extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and critics interested in depiction of nature
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles and evaluative criteria for depicting natural subjects (leafage, water, mountains, sunsets) in landscape painting and drawing, drawn from Ruskin's Modern Painters excerpts. Emphasizes observation of mass, light, colour, and transient effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leafage: celebrate variety and avoid exact repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves, though similar in form, never exactly repeat; the artist should not attempt to draw leaf-for-leaf uniformity but must capture the exquisite regularity modified by infinite variety—some leaves seen sideways, some foreshortened, some crossed, each differently turned and placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation guidance and anti-pattern: 'Break off an elm bough three feet long... try to draw it, leaf for leaf. It is ten to one if in the whole bough... you find one form of leaf exactly like another' — therefore avoid mechanical repetition; portray the disparate orientations, foreshortening and crossings that give the group its graceful disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leafage: render mass effects, transparency, and passages of light
rubrics_metrics.description: When foliage forms large masses the leaves at the extremities become fine and dust-like; the mass should be shown as transparent, with crumbling lights letting the sky through, and composed of illumined foliage contrasted with deep passages of broken irregular gloom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose foliage as layers: fine peripheral points, dazzling masses of light, deep shadow passages, twisted stems and shafted sunbeams 'running along the lustrous leaves for an instant.' Emphasize overall effect and penetrability rather than isolated detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leafage: use isolated leaves as types to convey character
rubrics_metrics.description: Here and there a single perfect leaf or a small symmetrical association should stand out as the 'type' that embodies the specific character of the group; such isolated motifs mark unity and grace without repeating the same form throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip: select one or two well-observed leaves to act as typifying elements at extremities or focal points; these give the viewer a sense of species and unity amid varied, almost chaotic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water (calm): indicate surface and reflection via careful projection and highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: To suggest the ordinary appearance of calm water, use careful curves of projection with a dark ground and break a little white over it to indicate reflection and surface detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example and technique: follow the practice of Ruysdael — emphasize curve, contrast and a few well-placed highlights rather than trying to render every micro-detail of the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water (animated): portray play of hue, motion, depth, and mixed reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: To depict running, falling or turbulent water (cataracts, sea-waves) the artist must render the play of hue on the reflective surface, the flashing velocity, ripples and wreaths, and the mingling of radiating sunbeams with the dim hues of transparent depth and dark rock below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is difficult and often beyond perfect execution; focus on capturing color variation, the precision and grace of motion, transparent depth, and the interplay of light and shadow that define dynamic water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water: perceive and choose the 'landscape in the water'
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost every pond or puddle contains a landscape in its reflection; the painter must consciously choose whether to show the water as refuse or as a mirror of sky and distant forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual advice: 'It is at your own will that you see in that despised stream either the refuse of the street, or the image of the sky.' Decide the scene's moral/aesthetic stance and depict the water accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountain colour: exploit massed colour and mountain-specific palette
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains introduce broad masses of purple, violet and ultramarine and delicate rose-colours at summits and dawn; the painter should use these large unbroken spaces of pure colour to achieve a depth and tenderness not seen in lowland landscapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour guidance: include distant violet and blue films, transitions into rose at peaks, and acknowledge the mountain's added palette when composing tonal relationships and atmospheric depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountain composition: show variety, redundance, layered visibility and richer incident detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains provide richer species of flower, more varied trees, abundant water features, and cloud effects; depict redundance (greater quantity of foliage), successive heights of trees clearly defined against sky, and a continual variety of incidents in stream, crag and cloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural advice: emphasize successive layers (tree after tree), clarity of forms against the sky, inlaid colour on stones, and numerous small 'incidents' (flowers, streams) that give mountains their superabundance of pictorial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clouds and sky in hill scenes: render multitudinous and novel cloud effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The mountain-scenery observer encounters cloud manifestations unseen in the lowlands; walking with and above the clouds produces effects (wreaths, pavements of moving marble, breaking against crags) that must be represented to convey hill-specific atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe mountain cloud behaviours: their scale, interaction with crags and snow, and the altered perception of sky when seen from elevations; incorporate these into composition and colour choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunset: capture transient, intense colour and fleeting opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme sunsets—especially the moment before the sun sinks when light turns pure rose—produce a molten sea of colour across zenith and horizon for only five to ten minutes; artists should be prepared to record these rare, intense chromatic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical and perceptual guidance: be aware of the rarity of such conditions (may occur only a few times a summer), the necessity of favourable vantage and readiness, and the difficulty of retaining degrees of colour in memory—work from observation while the effect lasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic honesty about limits: recognise some effects may be beyond perfect execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain complex effects—perfectly painting the actual play of hue on water or the full splendour of a great sunset—may be beyond human power; artists should aim for faithful partial success rather than illusion of complete mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical note: Ruskin concedes 'to do this perfectly is beyond the power of man; to do it even partially has been granted to but one or two,' advising humility and focused striving rather than overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable aesthetic qualities: prioritize colour, form, change and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty in landscape can be approached by 'calculation' — loveliness of colour, perfectness of form, endless change, and wonderfulness of structure are treatable as demonstrable, not purely subjective sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical stance: evaluate and compose landscapes with attention to these measurable qualities (colour richness, formal perfection, dynamic variation, structural complexity) rather than relying solely on vague feeling.
